claims.text: Greg Lavecchia (Bloom Nutrition, 2020) asserts that the word "restock" is the single most powerful word in marketing for physical DTC products that have previously sold out, because it simultaneously conveys three conversion signals: validity (the product was good enough to empty the warehouse), urgency (limited supply is available now), and FOMO (others missed it last time). Unlike generic scarcity language, "restock" requires a genuine prior sellout event to be credible.
claims.speaker: Greg Lavecchia
conditions: DTC physical product with a documented prior sellout event
Announcement made to an existing audience (email list, SMS list, social following)
claims.mechanism: A restock announcement converts three persuasion levers simultaneously: the past sellout is proof of quality (social proof), limited re-supply creates scarcity (urgency), and prior buyers who missed it experience loss aversion (FOMO). The word is a compressed proof-and-urgency signal that no manufactured scarcity phrase can replicate because it requires a real prior sellout.
bounded_by: Does not apply to products that have never sold out; the claim requires a genuine prior depletion event to carry the validity signal.
Does not apply to services or digital products where inventory does not constrain supply.

claims.text: Greg Lavecchia (Bloom Nutrition, 2020) argues that when a DTC founder discovers a product that demonstrably moves culture at scale, the correct capital allocation decision is to reinvest 100% of the proceeds into more product inventory rather than diversifying spending, because the discovered demand signal is the rarest business asset and must be exploited before competitors respond or consumer attention shifts.
claims.speaker: Greg Lavecchia
conditions: Product has produced a genuine sellout event indicating strong organic demand
Early-stage DTC founder (pre-scale, still proving product-market fit)
Capital is liquid and can be redeployed into inventory within weeks
claims.mechanism: A proven sellout event is time-limited evidence of demand; the window to capitalize closes as competitors observe and enter, or as consumer attention cycles. Reinvesting into supply extends the proven demand signal before it degrades.
bounded_by: Does not apply when unit economics of the product are unproven or negative.
Does not apply when supply chain lead times make restock impossible before demand window closes.

claims.text: Greg Lavecchia (Bloom Nutrition, 2020) demonstrates that simultaneous announcement across Instagram, email list, and SMS list for a restocked physical product can drive a complete sellout of 30,000 units and over $1 million in revenue within 12 hours, with only two full-time employees.
claims.speaker: Greg Lavecchia
conditions: Product had built accumulated demand and hype prior to announcement
Audience across Instagram, email, and SMS had been cultivated before launch

numbers.axis: units sold and revenue generated within 12 hours of restock announcement

bounded_by: Single data point from one product launch in 2020; no comparison cohort provided.
Result required prior accumulated demand and hype before restock; not repeatable without pre-built audience and prior sellout.

examples.text: In 2020, Greg Lavecchia and his wife were the only two full-time employees of Bloom Nutrition, operating out of a co-working space in Brooklyn, New York at age 24. After accumulating demand and hype for their greens powder, they received 25,000-30,000 bottles from their warehouse. They announced the restock simultaneously across Instagram, their email list, and their SMS list. Within 12 hours, all 30,000 bottles sold out, generating over $1 million in revenue. Lavecchia then took the entire proceeds and reinvested them into purchasing one million dollars worth of additional greens powder inventory rather than any other expense, treating the sellout as a validated signal to double down on the product.

practices.text: If you have a product that is genuinely affecting culture at scale and you strike a sellout event, go all in and double down on inventory rather than diversifying capital across other expenses.
